meta.name: Small Solar
meta.subtitle: A low-cost solar ladder for El Segundo, from one panel to a block
meta.rule: We point, the vendor sells. Nothing here is hosted, resold, or marked up. Prices are what a page said on the day we looked, and the day is written next to each one.
meta.sunNote: PVWatts for the weather station 1.7 km from LAX: a fixed south-facing 1 kW array at 20° tilt with the calculator's default 14% losses makes about 1,700 kWh a year, 4.6 kWh a day. The solar resource is 6.1 kWh per square metre a day, which is what a peak-sun hour is. The marine layer costs mornings in May and June; December is the low month at about 100 kWh per kW.

rungs.name: Pocket
rungs.line: One panel, one box, no wires past the desk.

storage.note: a 12 V 20–50 Ah LiFePO4 drop-in, or a small portable power station

runs: a router or a mesh node

parts.item: one 100–200 W panel, new or used
USB-C PD and 12 V sockets, inline fuse, MC4 leads

rungs.climb: Almost nothing carries up. Treat this rung as tuition, or buy a portable power station instead and it becomes the sneakernet battery on rung three.

rungs.name: Shed
rungs.line: Four used panels and a battery that runs a fridge.

storage.note: 24 V 100–200 Ah, or a single 48 V 100 Ah rack battery if you already know you are climbing

runs: a commons hub and a LoRa relay
rungs.permit: none while it stays a plug-in cord to portable loads; no hardwiring

parts.item: a 40–60 A MPPT controller, or an all-in-one inverter-charger
1–3 kW pure-sine inverter if not all-in-one
Class T fuse, DC breaker, 4–6 AWG wire, Anderson connectors, ground rod

rungs.climb: Buy 48 V-capable gear here and every part survives to the house rung. 12 V gear hits a wall around 1 kW of inverter.

rungs.name: House-critical
rungs.line: The loads you would miss in an outage, on their own panel.

storage.note: one or two 48 V 100 Ah server-rack batteries

runs: a heat-pump water heater on a good day
rungs.permit: yes: anything hardwired to the house needs a City of El Segundo electrical permit and a licensed electrician; a transfer switch or critical-loads subpanel is the safe shape

parts.item: 8–10 used panels or 5–6 new 450 W panels
5–10 kWh of 48 V rack LiFePO4, UL 1973 listed
critical-loads subpanel, transfer switch, rapid shutdown, labels

rungs.climb: Add strings and batteries in parallel. Nothing gets replaced, which is the whole point of picking 48 V two rungs ago.

rungs.name: Block
rungs.line: Several roofs, one shared battery, a hub that stays on.

storage.note: pooled rack batteries at the hub, plus portable stations that travel

runs: the resilience site for a few streets
rungs.permit: yes, and interconnection with Southern California Edison if anything can export; the sneakernet variant needs neither

parts.item: 10–20 kW of panels across the sunniest roofs
30–60 kWh of rack LiFePO4 at the hub
portable power stations as the batteries that walk
LoRa relay nodes on the sunniest roofs
a router, a Pi and a pair of roof radios per hop for the commons
a 48 V DC bus and PoE injectors to feed them

rungs.climb: Start this rung as a sneakernet: charge portable stations at the best roof, carry them to where power is needed. Wire the bus only after the pattern proves itself.

sizing.note: Store one to one and a half days of the loads you actually need after dark. Most people overbuy the battery and underbuy the panels. The 76% system efficiency is PVWatts' own default losses plus the inverter, so these are the numbers the sun leaves you, not a brochure.

loads.name: Wi-Fi commons hub: a Pi and a router

chemistry.name: LiFePO4
chemistry.body: Safe indoors, 3,000 to 6,000 cycles, flat under load, and roughly $150 to $250 per kWh for a listed pack. Look for UL 1973 on rack batteries and a BMS with a low-temperature charge cutoff.

chemistry.name: Sodium-ion
chemistry.body: Cheap and rugged, fine in cold, lower energy density. Worth pricing for the block rung by 2027, not worth waiting for on the small rungs.

chemistry.name: Lead-acid
chemistry.body: Half the usable capacity, a fifth of the cycle life, vents hydrogen. If someone gives you a set, use it outdoors and plan its replacement.

chemistry.name: Portable power stations
chemistry.verdict: buy for rungs zero and three
chemistry.body: A battery, inverter, MPPT and sockets in one UL-listed box. Costs more per kWh than a rack battery, needs no wiring or permit, and it carries. That last fact is what makes the block rung possible without trenching.

notBattery.name: Timing
notBattery.body: Run the dishwasher, laundry and e-bike charger on timers during sun hours. The battery only carries the night. This is the cheapest storage that exists.

notBattery.name: A chest freezer
notBattery.body: Fill the spare space with water jugs, let the inverter run it hard midday, and it coasts through the night on frozen mass.

notBattery.name: Hot water
notBattery.body: A DC heating element or a smart relay dumps surplus panel output into the tank instead of curtailing it. A heat-pump water heater on a timer is the same trick at three times the efficiency.

distribution.name: No wires
distribution.body: The loads live where the panel is. Rung zero needs nothing from anyone.

distribution.name: A 48 V DC bus and PoE
distribution.body: Run 48 V DC to fixed loads and use Power over Ethernet for mesh radios, cameras and small computers. USB-C PD adapters hang off the same bus. Under 60 V DC is generally treated as low voltage, which means far less permitting friction. Confirm with El Segundo Building Safety before it goes through walls.

distribution.name: Battery sneakernet
distribution.body: Charge portable stations at the sunniest roof and carry them to where the power is needed. Zero wiring and zero permits. For a block this works better than it sounds, and it is how rung three should start.

distribution.name: An AC island
distribution.body: An inverter feeds a critical-loads subpanel through a transfer switch. Once anything is hardwired to the house you need a permit and a licensed electrician. Never backfeed a panel without a transfer switch. It can kill a line worker.

distribution.name: The grid
distribution.body: Under NEM 3.0 the utility pays a fraction of retail for exports, so grid-tie without a battery barely pays. Anything that can export needs Southern California Edison interconnection. Plug-in solar is legal in Utah; California's rules are moving, so check the rules shelf before assuming.

safety: Fuse every battery lead at the battery. A Class T fuse on 48 V packs; the short-circuit current of LiFePO4 will weld an ordinary fuse shut.
DC-rated breakers or a disconnect between panels and controller. Solar DC arcs do not self-extinguish.
A BMS with low-temperature charge cutoff. Lithium plates below freezing; El Segundo rarely gets there, garages sometimes do.
A ground rod and bonded frames for any fixed array. Rapid shutdown and labels once it touches the house.
Never backfeed a house panel without a transfer switch. Suicide cords are named accurately.
Nothing on this page is electrical advice. Hardwired AC is a licensed electrician's job in California, and the permit protects you and the next owner.

shelves.title: Used and surplus panels
shelves.rule: Commercial take-offs run 10 to 20 cents a watt. Read the wattage sticker, check the frame and the glass. Snail trails are cosmetic; cracked glass is not.

items.name: SanTan Solar — used panels
items.sells: The largest used-panel reseller in the country, in Gilbert, Arizona. Pallets of 20 to 25 and a one-year warranty on used. Stock seen: SunPower 327 W, JA 310 W, Trina 240 W.
items.price: prices load in the browser; call or check the page

items.name: A1 SolarStore — Simi Valley pickup
items.sells: New and clearance panels, inverters and batteries with pickup inside 48 hours at the Simi Valley warehouse, the closest big desk to the South Bay.
items.price: clearance panels $150–250 each on the homepage

items.name: Surplus Solar Products
items.sells: Buys and sells used 335 to 465 W panels from Jinko, Q Cells and LG, plus inverters and racking, from warehouses in New York, California and Texas.

items.name: Surplus Record — California solar listings
items.sells: Industrial-surplus classifieds. On the day we looked, Turners Machinery in Santa Paula had REC and Mage panels listed.
items.price: $65 a panel, minimum six; ET Solar at $220

items.name: Craigslist Los Angeles — solar panels
items.sells: Two hundred-plus live listings across the basin: single panels, take-off lots and whole systems from Santa Clarita to Long Beach.

items.name: Facebook Marketplace — solar panels, Los Angeles
items.sells: The other local classifieds. Needs a login to see listings; we confirmed the category page, not the prices.

items.name: eBay — used solar panels
items.sells: National search for used and surplus modules. Freight on a pallet matters more than the sticker price here.

shelves.title: New panels and kits at wholesale desks
shelves.rule: The desks that sell to installers also sell to you. Free freight thresholds and pallet minimums decide the real price.

items.name: Watts247
items.sells: Affordable DIY solar: MPP Solar, Growatt, EG4 and Sol-Ark, rack batteries, and the cheapest new watts we found.
items.price: Longi 380 W bifacial at 26¢/W; Canadian Solar 695 W pallet $4,000

items.name: RENVU
items.sells: A California distributor since 2012: Sol-Ark, Enphase, Growatt, racking and balance-of-system parts.

items.name: Signature Solar
items.sells: Home of the EG4 brand: panels, inverters, batteries and kits from Texas. Free shipping over $4,000.
items.price: EG4 WallMount 280 Ah $2,700 on the banner

items.name: Northern Arizona Wind & Sun
items.sells: Selling off-grid gear since 1979, strong on MidNite, Victron and Sol-Ark, with people who answer the phone.

items.name: Current Connected
items.sells: Victron, EG4, SOK, Pytes and Sol-Ark, custom cables, and long product pages that explain the listings.

items.name: Shop Solar Kits
items.sells: Bundled kits and portable-station packages when you would rather not spec every part.
items.price: 100 W panel $89.99; 400 W foldable $599; EcoFlow Delta Pro kits from $1,899

items.name: altE Store
items.sells: Off-grid and DIY kits since 1999, quote-driven for anything past a single panel.

shelves.title: LiFePO4 batteries
shelves.rule: Look for UL 1973 on a rack battery and UL 9540 on a battery-plus-inverter system if it will ever touch a permit. Budget drop-ins are fine on the small rungs.

items.name: EG4 LifePower4 V2 — 48 V 100 Ah
items.sells: The 5.12 kWh server-rack battery the house rung is built on. Built-in breaker, ten-year warranty. The page states UL 1973 recognized, UL 9540A tested, UL 9540 listed.

items.name: SOK SK48V100N — 48 V 100 Ah
items.sells: A user-serviceable 3U rack battery with a heater and a seven-year warranty, shipped from a warehouse in Chino, California. No UL statement on the page.

items.name: EG4 WallMount — 280 and 314 Ah
items.sells: The 14 kWh indoor wall battery for a house that wants one box instead of a rack.

items.name: LiTime
items.sells: Budget 12, 24 and 48 V drop-ins, formerly Ampere Time. The 48 V ComFlex talks to Victron gear.

items.name: Redodo
items.sells: Budget 12 V 100 Ah drop-ins for the pocket and shed rungs.

items.name: Battle Born
items.sells: The premium 12 V drop-in, assembled in Reno with a ten-year warranty. You pay for the support line.

items.name: Docan Power — prismatic cells
items.sells: EVE and CATL prismatic LiFePO4 cells from Texas stock for people building their own packs. Sixteen-cell minimum.
items.price: EVE 280 Ah $94, 304 Ah $103 a cell, about 11¢/Wh

items.name: Battery Hookup
items.sells: Salvage and new cells, modules and BMS boards. Where the cheapest watt-hours live if you can solder.

items.name: 18650 Battery Store
items.sells: Samsung and Molicel cylindrical cells and EVE MB31 prismatics from Georgia.

shelves.title: Controllers and inverters
shelves.rule: One all-in-one at 48 V replaces three boxes. Victron costs more and lasts; EG4 and MPP are the value line. Anything hardwired wants UL 1741 on the label.

items.name: EG4 6000XP
items.sells: The 6 kW split-phase all-in-one the house rung assumes: 8 kW of PV in, 48 V battery, UL 1741 certificate on the page.

items.name: EG4 3000EHV-48
items.sells: The 3 kW 120 V all-in-one for the shed rung: 5 kW of PV, 500 V MPPT, parallels to twelve later.

items.name: MPP Solar and Humless — via Watts247
items.sells: The value line of all-in-ones. The Humless LVX6048WP is a 6 kW outdoor split-phase unit with UL 1741.
items.price: LVX6048WP $1,199 on sale; LV6548 plus 15 kWh bundle $3,499

items.name: Victron — Bay Marine Supply, San Diego
items.sells: A Victron True Blue distributor two hours south, with 199 Victron parts on the shelf and a counter.

items.name: Victron — Blue Marine
items.sells: The full Victron range with free shipping over $49.

items.name: Renogy
items.sells: The 12 V starter brand: Rover MPPT controllers, small panels, sockets and cables for the pocket rung.
items.price: Rover Li MPPT from $87.99; 100 W panel from $109.99

items.name: Victron — where to buy
items.sells: Victron's own dealer map, for finding the counter nearest you.

shelves.title: Portable power stations
shelves.rule: A battery, inverter, MPPT and sockets in one listed box. Dearer per kWh than a rack, but it needs no wiring, no permit, and it carries. Rung zero and the sneakernet run on these.

items.name: Anker SOLIX
items.sells: The C1000 (1 kWh) and S2000 (2 kWh) are the sneakernet workhorses; LiFePO4 inside.
items.price: S2000 $999.99; C1000 seen at $430–479 on sale elsewhere

items.name: EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max — 2,048 Wh
items.sells: 2 kWh LiFePO4 with 2,400 W out and fast solar input. Pre-order shipping mid-October when seen.

items.name: EcoFlow DELTA 3 — 1,024 Wh
items.sells: The 1 kWh box for the pocket rung. The old DELTA 2 page now sells the DELTA 3.

items.name: Bluetti AC180 — 1,152 Wh
items.sells: 1.15 kWh LiFePO4 with 1,800 W out, the usual price leader in this size.
items.price: $499, out of stock until late November when seen

shelves.title: Wiring and the parts that stop fires
shelves.rule: Genuine MC4, Anderson for anything you unplug, a Class T fuse at the battery, DC-rated breakers, real copper. This shelf is cheap; skipping it is not.

items.name: Stäubli MC4 pair
items.sells: The genuine connector, 12 to 10 AWG, 25-year warranty. Counterfeit MC4s are where roof fires start.

items.name: Anderson SB50 and SB175 — Bend Battery
items.sells: The plug for anything that comes off the bus: battery leads, portable loads, the sneakernet.

items.name: Powerwerx — Anderson SB connectors
items.sells: The canonical Anderson source, in Brea, Orange County. The site blocks robots; we confirmed the page, not the price.

items.name: Blue Sea 5502 Class T fuse block
items.sells: The fuse block for a 48 V lithium bank, 225 to 400 A, 160 V DC. Fuse sold separately. San Diego counter.

items.name: MidNite Solar MNEPV DC breakers — via NAZ
items.sells: 150 V DC DIN-rail breakers from 1 to 63 A between the panels and the controller.

items.name: WindyNation welding cable
items.sells: US-made pure-copper battery cable from 8 to 4/0 AWG, with back-door pickup at the Ventura warehouse.

items.name: TEMCo 2 AWG welding cable, 50 ft
items.sells: US-made 205 A EPDM cable with free shipping, for the runs between battery, fuse and inverter.

items.name: PoE Texas 8-port 48 V injector
items.sells: Puts eight radios or cameras on a 48 V bank with one box. The DC-bus distribution rung starts here.

items.name: UltraPoE PoE-N912-2SL48
items.sells: 12 to 48 V DC in, 802.3at PoE+ out, DIN rail, rated to 80 °C, built for standalone solar cabinets.

shelves.title: LoRa mesh radios
shelves.rule: Buy nRF52 for anything unattended, ESP32 for the desk. Rokland in Florida is the US counter; the makers ship from Shenzhen and sell out.

items.name: RAK WisBlock Meshtastic starter kit — US915
items.sells: The nRF52840 node that runs for weeks on a cell, pre-flashed, solar input on the base board. The relay we would put on a roof.

items.name: Seeed SenseCAP T1000-E card
items.sells: A credit-card LoRa node with GPS and a week of battery, IP65. The one you hand to a neighbour who will never open a settings screen.

items.name: Seeed SenseCAP Solar Node P1-Pro
items.sells: The turnkey rooftop repeater: 5 W panel, four 18650 cells, GPS, nRF52 and an RP-SMA socket for a real antenna. Eight to nine km in the open, says the maker.

items.name: Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V3 — Rokland
items.sells: The entry ESP32 board with a screen, the one every tutorial uses. Fine on a desk, hungry on a roof.

items.name: Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V4 — Rokland
items.sells: The V3 with a stronger radio, a solar connector on the board and deep sleep under 20 µA. Needs recent firmware.

items.name: LILYGO T-Beam and T-Echo series — Rokland
items.sells: GPS boards with an 18650 holder, the e-paper T-Echo, and the keyboard T-Deck, in US stock while the maker’s own store was sold out.

items.name: LILYGO T-Echo — maker’s store
items.sells: The nRF52840 e-paper node with GNSS, direct from Shenzhen. Sold out when seen.

items.name: Rokland 5.8 dBi outdoor 915 MHz antenna kit
items.sells: The fiberglass omni and cable that turn a $35 node into the relay the block can hear.

items.name: Heltec — maker’s store
items.sells: The V3 direct, cheaper and slower, with a US warehouse option on some listings.

items.name: Adafruit LoRa boards
items.sells: Feather RFM95 boards and the Pi LoRa bonnet for RNode and experiments. Not first-class Meshtastic targets, and no Heltec or RAK stock.

shelves.title: The commons: routers, roof radios, the hub
shelves.rule: A travel router with the WAN unplugged, a Pi beside it, and a pair of roof radios per hop. All of it runs on 5 V or passive PoE from the 48 V bus.

items.name: GL.iNet Mango GL-MT300N-V2
items.sells: A 40-gram OpenWrt router that draws under 3 W. The cheapest commons that exists.

items.name: GL.iNet Opal GL-SFT1200
items.sells: Dual-band AC1200 with three gigabit ports for a house-sized commons, USB-C powered.

items.name: GL.iNet Beryl AX GL-MT3000
items.sells: Wi-Fi 6 with a 2.5 Gb port, measured under 3.5 W in use. The commons router for a hub that serves video.

items.name: Ubiquiti NanoStation 5AC Loco
items.sells: The 5 GHz roof-to-roof radio, 13 dBi, 24 V passive PoE, 7 W. Two of these are one hop of a street.

items.name: MikroTik SXTsq 5 ac
items.sells: The other roof radio, 16 dBi, RouterOS, 7 W. What NYC Mesh hangs.

items.name: Raspberry Pi 5 — official page
items.sells: The hub. Idles at 2.4 to 3.3 W, ten flat out; wants the 27 W supply.

items.name: Raspberry Pi 5 8 GB — PiShop
items.sells: The US reseller that had the 8 GB board in stock and cheapest when seen.

items.name: Raspberry Pi 5 — Adafruit
items.sells: Adafruit’s listing, with cases, supplies and the cards to go with it.

items.name: Kiwix Wikipedia files
items.sells: The ZIM files the hub serves. Full English with pictures was 119 GB in the August 2026 edition; the no-picture editions are a tenth of that.

rules.name: El Segundo automated residential solar permitting (SolarAPP+)
rules.body: The city is in the SolarAPP+ pilot: instant permits for roof-mounted PV and storage on single-family homes, applied for and paid online by a licensed contractor. The city site blocks robots, so we confirmed the address through the search index. Open it in a browser.

rules.name: El Segundo Building and Safety Division
rules.body: The counter for anything SolarAPP+ does not cover: ground mounts, subpanels, transfer switches, a DC bus through a wall. Ask before you drill.

rules.name: SCE Solar Billing Plan (what people call NEM 3.0)
rules.body: Export credits run roughly 3 to 23 cents a kWh depending on hour and season, highest 4 to 9 pm in June through September, plus a small residential adder. Storage is what makes exports worth anything. The interconnection request lives on this page.

rules.name: SCE net energy metering (closed to new applicants)
rules.body: NEM 2.0 closed on April 15, 2023. New systems go to the Solar Billing Plan. The application fee for systems under 1 MW was $94 when seen.

rules.name: CPUC customer generation and net billing
rules.body: The regulator’s own page on the Net Billing Tariff in force since April 15, 2023. The CPUC never calls it NEM 3.0; the utilities and everyone else do.

rules.name: California Solar Consumer Protection Guide
rules.body: Version 4, 2025, in nine languages. Any solar provider in California must hand it to you at first contact. Read it before you sign anything, including a lease.

rules.name: Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP)
rules.body: The Residential Solar and Storage Equity budget opened June 2, 2025 with $1,100 per kWh of storage and $3,100 per kW of solar for qualifying low-income households, $280 million in all. Installer-applied, not DIY.

rules.name: SGIP applicant portal
rules.body: The 2026 SGIP handbook, the step tracker and the waitlists. Southern California Edison is the program administrator for El Segundo.

rules.name: GoGreen Home energy financing
rules.body: State-backed loans for solar, batteries and efficiency with no lien on the house, open to SCE and SoCalGas customers, owners and renters with permission. It has a do-it-yourself section, which is rare.

rules.name: SB 868, the Plug and Play Solar Act — on the Governor’s desk
rules.body: Passed the Assembly 73 to 0 on August 25 and the Senate 36 to 4 on August 26, enrolled to the Governor August 31, 2026. Deadline to sign or veto is September 30. Not signed when seen. If signed: up to 1,200 W AC per dwelling plugged into a standard receptacle, no interconnection application or fee, certified anti-backfeed equipment, effective January 1, 2027, sunset January 1, 2030. Until then plug-in solar is a grey area here.

rules.name: Plug-in solar explainer — Solar Rights Alliance
rules.body: The plain-language page on what SB 868 does and does not allow, kept current by the group that carried it.

rules.name: Utah HB 340 — the first US plug-in solar law
rules.body: Signed March 25, 2025, in force May 7, 2025. Up to 1,200 W AC at the inverter into a standard 120 V outlet, anti-islanding required, no permit or utility approval, no net metering. Passed 72 to 0 and 27 to 0. It is the template California’s bill follows.

rules.name: IRS: the 25D residential clean energy credit ended
rules.body: No credit for expenditures after December 31, 2025, and an expenditure counts when the installation is completed, not when you paid. Credits earned before 2026 can still be carried forward. Price the ladder without it.

rules.name: 47 CFR 15.247 — the license-free 902–928 MHz band
rules.body: Meshtastic, MeshCore and RNode radios operate here under Part 15: no licence, up to 1 W conducted for digital modulation, encryption allowed. Meshtastic caps North America at +30 dBm ERP. The eCFR itself blocks robots; this is Cornell’s mirror.

rules.name: 47 CFR 97.113 — no obscured messages on amateur bands
rules.body: Amateur radio forbids messages encoded to obscure their meaning, which is why an AREDN mesh cannot carry encrypted chat or HTTPS the way a Part 15 mesh can. Use the ham backbone for what it is good at and keep the phones on 915 MHz and Wi-Fi.

rules.name: ARRL — getting a Technician licence
rules.body: Thirty-five questions and a $35 FCC application fee, good for ten years. The door to AREDN and to the Mt. Wilson links the South Bay hams already run.

learn.name: DIY Solar Power Forum
learn.body: 1.9 million posts from 173,000 people who have made every mistake first. The marketplace subforum is a real source of used gear.

learn.name: Will Prowse’s approved shop
learn.body: The list behind the most-watched DIY solar channel, split into certified permit-ready gear and budget gear. His affiliate links, not ours.

learn.name: Off-Grid Garage
learn.body: Andy in Australia tears down LiFePO4 cells and BMS boards on camera. Watch before you buy a battery you cannot open.

learn.name: PVWatts
learn.body: The free production model behind every number on this page. The lab was renamed the National Laboratory of the Rockies; the old nrel.gov address no longer resolves.

learn.name: Global Solar Atlas
learn.body: World Bank and Solargis maps of solar yield anywhere on earth. Be careful which pixel you click; a Mojave point is often quoted for Los Angeles.

learn.name: EnergySage
learn.body: Installer quotes and equipment comparisons, for the day the ladder stops being a hobby and needs a contractor.

learn.name: Solar Power World on the secondhand market
learn.body: Why used modules sell 50 to 75 percent below new, and who trades them at scale.

learn.name: Meshtastic — solar-powered nodes
learn.body: How to measure what a node actually draws before you size its panel. Some nodes sit at 25 mW.

learn.name: Jeff Geerling on Pi 5 power
learn.body: The measured idle and load numbers behind the hub row above.

method: Every price is what a vendor's own page said on the day written next to it. Prices move; the day is the fact.
Every link goes to the seller or the agency, never a middle page. We point, the vendor sells.
The yields are PVWatts v8 numbers for the weather station 1.7 km from LAX with the calculator's default losses, not a sunny-day brochure. The run is in the JSON twin.
The rungs are budgets, not kits. Parts on each rung name a shelf, and the shelf names the vendors.
Rules are dated. California and the federal credit both changed in 2025 and 2026; the rules shelf says what we could verify and when.
Nothing here is inside information, sponsorship, or an affiliate link.

mesh.line: A network that stays up when the wire goes down.
mesh.intro: The internet is a wire someone else owns. A local network is the same phones and laptops talking to each other over the air, and it runs on the same small solar as everything else on this page. Three layers, cheapest first. Each one works on its own; together they cover a block.

layers.name: Phone to phone, no hardware
layers.reach: a room, a courtyard, a queue
layers.body: Apps that use Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct to pass messages from phone to phone, hopping through whoever is in range. Nothing to buy, nothing to install on a roof. iPhones and Androids do not always see each other, so pick one app the whole block agrees on.

phones.iphone: yes: Bitchat, Berty, OSHI. Not Briar, not Meshenger

layers.name: LoRa mesh nodes
layers.reach: a few miles line of sight, a mile through houses
layers.body: Pocket radios on the license-free 915 MHz band that carry short text and positions between phones over miles, hopping node to node. A node runs for days on a small battery and forever on a palm-sized panel. Every phone pairs to a node over Bluetooth with a free app. This is the layer that reaches the whole block for the price of a dinner each.

phones.iphone: yes: the Meshtastic and MeshCore apps, paired to a node over Bluetooth
phones.linux: yes: CLI, web client, runs a node

layers.name: A Wi-Fi commons
layers.reach: a house, a yard, a street with roof links
layers.body: A router with no wire in the back and a small computer beside it. Phones join the network the way they join any Wi-Fi, and instead of the internet they find a local page, a shared drive, offline Wikipedia and a chat room. Roof radios link one commons to the next. This is where a copy of PointCast could live when the wire is gone.

phones.iphone: yes: stays joined to a no-internet Wi-Fi; grant Local Network permission
phones.linux: yes, and it runs the hub

layers.name: One fabric over all of it
layers.body: Software that treats LoRa, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and a stray internet link as one encrypted network, so a message typed on the commons reaches a LoRa node three roofs away. Runs on a Pi or a laptop, free.

phones.iphone: TestFlight beta only, no App Store client yet
phones.android: yes: Sideband APK, no Play listing
phones.linux: yes: Sideband, MeshChat, rnsd on a Pi

apps.name: Bitchat
apps.body: Bluetooth mesh chat with no accounts and no phone numbers, up to a handful of hops, encrypted with the Noise protocol. Version 1.7 on the App Store when seen. No outside security audit yet.

apps.name: Berty
apps.body: Bluetooth, local Wi-Fi and Apple Multipeer under an encrypted-by-default protocol from a Paris non-profit. Alive and shipping; its own README says not yet for sensitive data.

apps.name: OSHI
apps.body: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct mesh with a Linux desktop client, LoRa radio support and an optional relay. Version 1.0, small and new: treat as unaudited.

apps.name: Briar
apps.body: The veteran: Bluetooth, local Wi-Fi and Tor, everything stored on the phone. Android only, and the developers say no iPhone client is planned. In maintenance mode since July 2026, security fixes only.

apps.name: Bridgefy
apps.body: Bluetooth mesh with the Signal protocol. The catch for an outage: it needs the internet to log in, and reviewers report being logged out when the wire is gone.

apps.name: Meshtastic
apps.body: The open LoRa mesh: AES-256 channels, phones paired over Bluetooth, a web client and a flasher in the browser, a Python CLI for a Pi. The ground range record is 331 km. SoCal Mesh runs on it with non-default settings, see the groups.

apps.name: MeshCore
apps.body: The younger LoRa mesh with companion, repeater and room-server roles and an open-source client on every platform. Fifty-plus boards including the Heltec V3 and the T-Deck. RegionMesh runs Los Angeles on it.

apps.name: Reticulum and RNode
apps.body: The encrypted network stack that makes a LoRa radio, a Wi-Fi link and a stray internet connection one fabric. RNode firmware turns the same Heltec, LILYGO and RAK boards into Reticulum interfaces. Layer four lives here.

apps.name: Sideband
apps.body: The Reticulum messenger: sideloaded on Android, an AppImage or pip on a Pi. No app-store listing. The iPhone build is a TestFlight beta that only networks in the foreground.

apps.name: Reticulum MeshChat
apps.body: A web page on the commons that is a chat room, a file drop and voice over Reticulum. Phones use it in a browser, which is how iPhones get on layer four today.

apps.name: OpenWrt
apps.body: The Linux that runs the router. Turn off the WAN and the same box is a commons. Every GL.iNet on the shelf ships with it under the hood; LibreMesh and AREDN are built on it.

apps.name: LibreMesh
apps.body: OpenWrt firmware for a multi-hop community mesh across roofs, batman-adv underneath, one network name for the whole block.

apps.name: Kiwix
apps.body: Offline Wikipedia and more, served from a Pi to every phone on the commons. The full English Wikipedia file was 119 GB when seen; the no-pictures editions fit a small card.

apps.name: Syncthing
apps.body: The shared drive with no server: every device keeps a copy and they sync over the local network. The original Android app was archived in 2024; use the Fork.

apps.name: Meshenger
apps.body: Voice and video calls between phones on the same commons with no server at all, contacts swapped by QR code. Android only.

apps.name: Conduit
apps.body: A single-binary Matrix chat server that runs on a Pi, so the block can use the Matrix apps it already knows, against a room that lives on the hub.

nodes.name: LoRa node, nRF52 board (RAK, T-Echo, T1000-E, Seeed Solar Node)
nodes.note: measured 4.5–7.5 mA receiving; a 3,000 mAh cell lasts two to four weeks of June gloom with no sun

nodes.name: LoRa node, ESP32 board (Heltec, T-Beam)
nodes.note: far hungrier than nRF52; fine on a wall wart, wrong for an unattended roof

nodes.name: GL.iNet Mango as the commons router
nodes.note: the spec sheet maximum; 5 V USB

nodes.name: Raspberry Pi 5 as the hub
nodes.note: idle, measured; about 10 W flat out; a 2 GB board idles at 2.4 W

nodes.name: Ubiquiti Loco5AC roof radio, one end
nodes.note: the spec maximum; 24 V passive PoE

method: Agree on one app per layer before the outage, and test it on a sunny afternoon when nothing is wrong. For a block with iPhones that means Bitchat or Berty on layer one, and a LoRa node in every third pocket.

Build the LoRa layer first: it costs the least, reaches the furthest, and needs the least power. Buy nRF52 boards for anything unattended and spend the antenna money; the stock whips are near useless.
To join SoCal Mesh, set LongTurbo, slot 14, region US. A default node hears nothing.
A commons without content is a blinking light. Put Kiwix, a map, the shared drive and a chat room on the Pi before the wire goes down. Plan a 256 GB card if you want the whole Wikipedia.

iPhones stay joined to a Wi-Fi with no internet, but every local app asks for Local Network permission the first time, and the phone may quietly prefer cellular. If a page will not load, Airplane Mode then Wi-Fi back on.
Encryption is fine on the license-free 915 MHz band under FCC Part 15. It is forbidden on amateur bands under Part 97, which is why AREDN is a licensed backbone and not a commons for phones.

groups.name: SoCal Mesh
groups.body: Hundreds of Meshtastic nodes across LA, Orange County, the Inland Empire and San Diego. They run the LongTurbo preset on slot 14 (908.750 MHz), region US, so a factory-default node will not see them until you change it. Discord is the door; the live map shows the MQTT-connected nodes.

groups.name: RegionMesh — MeshCore Los Angeles
groups.body: The MeshCore network for the basin. Downtown, the Westside and the Valley are the busy parts; the South Bay is listed as expanding.

groups.name: Meshtastic local groups
groups.body: The official list, with Laguna, Mission Viejo and the Orange County canyons alongside SoCal Mesh.

groups.name: AREDN — the licensed backbone
groups.body: Amateur-radio mesh on roof radios, linking the South Bay to Mt. Wilson. Needs a Technician licence and forbids encryption on the air, so it is a backbone for licensed neighbours, not a commons for phones.

groups.name: NYC Mesh wiki
groups.body: The best-documented community network in the country: how they hang MikroTik and Ubiquiti radios, what fails, what to buy.
